page_placements.theme: Optimisation and data-statistics artifact latents (dense, unigram, position-locked)

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how feature input specificity changes with SAE size, a related test of V1, but it does not map smaller features to larger features or test whether their inputs partition or their directions remain close.
record.gate_note: The size trend in Figure 9 bears on feature specificity as dictionary size increases. The other included results measure unigram-related feature behavior, not feature splitting or parent-child correspondence.
record.test_reason: Figure 9 runs Bloom's GPT-2 small layer-8 feature-splitting SAE series at several dictionary sizes. The text states that as SAE size increases, each feature is strongly activated by fewer unigrams. That is a population-level measure of features getting finer with dictionary size, which bears on V1. The study does not match features across sizes, check input coverage, or measure direction proximity.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that many RES-JB SAE features mainly reconstruct common unigrams and bigrams (an estimated 35–45% unigram, about 70% bigram). They attribute this to training-data frequency imbalance. Their proposed fix, a per-token lookup bias (Tokenized SAEs), gives better sparse-regime reconstruction, faster training and, in a small preliminary manual study, more complex features.
record.recipe_differences: Measures unigram activation specificity across SAE sizes and compares tokenized with non-tokenized SAEs; it does not perform feature correspondence or split-partition analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature specificity varies with SAE size; the study also reports effects from adding a per-token lookup table.

fits_no_version.finding: Many RES-JB layer-8 features respond to unigrams: of the 76% activated by a unigram, 39% match the top unigram and 66% match at least one. The authors estimate 35–45% of features reconstruct common unigrams.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A large share of SAE features encode common token and n-gram statistics, driven by training-data frequency imbalance.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a per-token lookup bias cuts unigram-specific features to under 5% and lowers encoder similarity to unigram inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separating token reconstruction from the dictionary reduces unigram-related SAE features.

record.problems: The dictionary-size trend is reported qualitatively, with numerical values shown only in a figure; it does not identify matched features across sizes or measure input partitioning and direction proximity. The authors also describe the manual feature study as limited and preliminary.

untested.parts: Mapping coarse features to finer ones across sizes; whether the finer features together cover the coarse feature's inputs; whether their directions lie near the coarse direction.
All of it: no splitting analysis in Pythia-1.4B or across SAE families.
All of it: no nested families, geometry or concept hierarchy.
All of it: no parent/child firing gaps.
All of it: no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no novel-latent analysis.
Splitting as an objective artifact is not tested. The authors attribute unigram features to training-data imbalance instead, and do not test Matryoshka SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: The link to feature splitting is incidental. The study uses Bloom's feature-splitting SAE series only for the Figure 9 specificity trend. The paper's main claims concern token-statistics features and a new SAE architecture.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not map features across dictionary sizes, test whether finer features partition a coarse feature's inputs, or measure whether their directions are nearby.
The Pythia experiments compare tokenized and non-tokenized SAE reconstruction, not splitting across SAE sizes or families.
No nested feature families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy are tested.
The study does not test parent-child firing gaps or whether changes to SAE size or sparsity fix them.
The study does not test whether larger latents decompose into smaller latents or whether larger SAEs add novel latents.

The study attributes unigram and n-gram feature behavior to training-data imbalance and proposes tokenized SAEs, but does not test whether feature splitting is an artifact of the sparsity objective or compare Matryoshka SAEs.

statements.problem: The part about this study is right. §5.1 says a smaller set of unigrams activates each feature as SAE size increases. The >5 threshold is in the Figure 9 caption, the values are figure-only, and no features are matched across sizes. The Gemma part belongs to another study and was not checked here.

The text gives 76%, 39% and 66% for RES-JB layer 8. It gives 35-45% as the authors' estimate for RES-JB features in general (not layer-specific; the statement doesn't say it is). The 'under 5%' is for the tokenized SAEs from Figure 7 (features activating on any single unigram). The authors themselves present this as a reduction.
